input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-603: Computational Problem Solving. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Assignments (both in class and homework) requiring a pseudo-code solution and implementation in a programming language are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-603]
This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Assignments (both in class and homework) requiring a pseudo-code solution and implementation in a programming language are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: CSCI-603 is a graduate bridge course that applies computational thinking through a problem-centered approach, focusing on algorithms, data structures, recursion, and debugging.
beats.example: Students in COMPSCI-MS will solve structured problems using pseudo-code and a programming language, with assignments requiring both representations.
beats.title: 1. Course Context & Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a course roadmap graphic showing the ten teaching beats arranged linearly, with a badge indicating 'Graduate Bridge Course (COMPSCI-MS only)' and a note about permission requirements for undergraduates.

beats.claim: A disciplined solution requires three sequential phases: stating inputs and outputs, proving correctness, and analyzing time and space resource bounds.
beats.example: For a sorting problem, the claim specifies 'sort an array of integers', the proof verifies each element ends in non-decreasing order, and the analysis shows O(n log n) time and O(1) space.
beats.title: 2. Disciplined Solution Framework
beats.visualDirection: Show a three-step flowchart labeled 'Inputs/Outputs', 'Correctness Proof', and 'Resource Analysis', with arrows indicating the mandatory sequence.

beats.claim: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds using asymptotic notation to describe how resource use grows with input.
beats.example: If input size doubles, a linear scan's time doubles, while a binary search's time increases by only one additional step, illustrating asymptotic growth.
beats.title: 3. Algorithm Analysis & Asymptotics
beats.visualDirection: Render a graph comparing two curves: one linear (O(n)) and one logarithmic (O(log n)), with a legend explaining how asymptotic notation captures growth rates.

beats.claim: A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination, ensuring the loop produces the correct result without infinite execution.
beats.example: In a sum loop, the invariant 'sum equals the total of elements processed so far' holds before each iteration, after each update, and when the loop ends.
beats.title: 4. Loop Invariants & Correctness
beats.visualDirection: Display a loop structure with three callouts: 'Initialization (before loop)', 'Maintenance (inside loop)', and 'Termination (after loop)', each linked to the invariant statement.

beats.claim: Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine their results to form the final solution.
beats.example: Merging two sorted lists involves dividing the combined list into halves, recursively sorting each half, and then merging the sorted halves back together.
beats.title: 5. Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a binary tree where the root is the full problem, children are subproblems, and leaves are base cases, with arrows showing the 'divide', 'solve', and 'combine' phases.

beats.claim: Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms by expressing the total cost in terms of the cost of smaller subproblems plus the work done at each level.
beats.example: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes merge sort, where the cost is twice the cost of sorting half the input plus linear time to merge.
beats.title: 6. Recurrence Relations & Cost
beats.visualDirection: Show a recursive call tree with labeled nodes, each node's cost calculated using the recurrence formula, and a summary box showing the total cost formula.

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations, while stacks use last-in, first-out access to manage ordered data efficiently.
beats.example: A stack of function calls pushes new tasks onto the top and pops the most recently added task first, ensuring LIFO behavior during recursion.
beats.title: 7. Elementary Data Structures: Lists & Stacks
beats.visualDirection: Draw two side-by-side diagrams: a horizontal list with index pointers and a vertical stack with a 'top' marker and push/pop arrows.

beats.claim: Queues use first-in, first-out access, trees represent hierarchical relationships supporting recursive traversals, and hash tables map keys to locations using collision strategies.
beats.example: A queue processes tasks in arrival order, a binary tree organizes data hierarchically with parent-child links, and a hash table stores key-value pairs with a fallback strategy for duplicate keys.
beats.title: 8. Elementary Data Structures: Queues, Trees, & Hash Tables
beats.visualDirection: Create a composite graphic showing a queue with 'front' and 'rear' markers, a tree with root/branch/leaf labels, and a hash table with key buckets and collision chains.

beats.claim: Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms, enabling solutions to reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions.
beats.example: An adjacency list for a city map stores each intersection as a vertex and roads as edges, allowing algorithms to find the shortest route between two locations.
beats.title: 9. Graphs & Reachability
beats.visualDirection: Render a network graph with labeled vertices and directed edges, highlighting a path from start to end node, and annotate the adjacency list representation below.

beats.claim: Effective computational problem solving requires verifying inputs, validating outputs, checking invariants, and applying systematic debugging and testing to ensure correctness and
beats.example: Before running code, verify the input matches the specification, check that the output matches expected results, confirm loop invariants hold, and use test cases to catch edge cases.
beats.title: 10. Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with four boxes: 'Verify Inputs', 'Validate Outputs', 'Check Invariants', 'Debug & Test', each with a checkbox and a brief action prompt.

learningObjectives: Define and apply the core components of a disciplined solution: problem specification, correctness argument, and resource bounds.
Represent and manipulate elementary data structures (lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, graphs) using appropriate invariants and access rules.
Formulate and execute a problem-solving workflow that integrates pseudo-code expression, recursive decomposition, and systematic debugging/testing.

Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Stress-test the reasoning around 7. Elementary Data Structures: Lists & Stacks with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Consider this worked case: A stack of function calls pushes new tasks onto the top and pops the most recently added task first, ensuring LIFO behavior during recursion. On screen, draw two side-by-side diagrams: a horizontal list with index pointers and a vertical stack with a 'top' marker and push/pop arrows. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

Next, compare the choices involved in 4. Loop Invariants & Correctness and make the decision criteria explicit. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Consider this worked case: In a sum loop, the invariant 'sum equals the total of elements processed so far' holds before each iteration, after each update, and when the loop ends. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

Examine the tradeoffs in 6. Recurrence Relations & Cost, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes merge sort, where the cost is twice the cost of sorting half the input plus linear time to merge. On screen, show a recursive call tree with labeled nodes, each node's cost calculated using the recurrence formula, and a summary box showing the total cost formula. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Use 8. Elementary Data Structures: Queues, Trees, & Hash Tables to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Consider this worked case: A queue processes tasks in arrival order, a binary tree organizes data hierarchically with parent-child links, and a hash table stores key-value pairs with a fallback strategy for duplicate keys.
